The hardest decision of my day happens at about six forty in the morning, before most of the building is awake. It is whether to hold the first departure. And the thing people outside this room never believe is that I do not have the information yet. I will not have it for another half an hour. If I wait until I am certain, the window has closed and the weather has made the decision for me, and the weather is not accountable to anybody. So I decide early, on incomplete information, and then I keep a backup plan for the decision I have just made. The other thing I want to say is about delays. Announcing a one hour delay does not fix anything. The aircraft is still where it was. The crew is still in traffic. What it does is buy time, and buying time is very often the only move available to me. But be careful with it. Buy time twice and you have bought yourself an afternoon. Buy it four times and you have moved the whole problem into the evening, and now it belongs to somebody else.

There is an experiment from the nineteen nineties that has been repeated so many times it is almost boring, and the result never moves. Researchers asked final year students to predict when they would finish their thesis. Not the optimistic date. The realistic one. On average they said thirty four days. The real average was fifty six, and fewer than half of them were finished by the day they had been confident about. Now here is the part that makes it interesting rather than depressing. When the same students were asked to predict how long a friend would take, they were remarkably accurate. The optimism only appears when the plan belongs to you. It is not laziness and it is not vanity. It is that when you imagine your own project you imagine the path where nothing goes wrong, because that is the only path you can picture in detail. Everybody else's delays are visible to you. Your own are hypothetical. The fix that actually works is almost insultingly simple. Stop asking how long this will take, and start asking how long the last five things like it actually took.
